headline: High-risk default write-and-network pair: Plandex can modify local code while the other agent is an unverified docs-only content tool with broad egress, creating dangerous interaction and compliance uncertainty.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: A is a content-writing agent with no shared channel or parser surface shown, while B reads/writes project files and can execute shell. The only plausible bridge is manual or file-based handoff, so injection is possible but not default. Uncertainty remains because A’s I/O surfaces are empty and B’s file ingestion is documented.
conditions: IF A’s text is copied into files that B later reads as instructions
IF B is configured to treat repository text as authoritative prompts
mitigations: Use a strict prompt/template separator for any A→B handoff
Require B to summarize and verify A output before acting
Keep A outputs in a non-executable notes file
Disable auto-apply in B for any content sourced from A

B_data_leakage.rationale: B has broad network egress and reads the filesystem, so any sensitive source code or secrets in its workspace can leave the machine. A is docs-only and touches no data classes, but its broad egress means pairwise leakage risk is still driven by B’s default ability to transmit local file contents to external services.
conditions: IF sensitive files are present in B’s project directory
IF B sends file contents to Plandex Cloud or a model provider
mitigations: Remove secrets from the workspace before running B
Point B at a scrubbed test repository
Use a local-only model/provider configuration if available
Restrict outbound network at the OS or container level
Review B’s upload settings before each run

C_capability_conflict.rationale: B can write the filesystem and modify git state, and its concurrency model says shared state exists via the Plandex server backend. A has no write capability shown, so direct conflict is one-sided, but B’s own multi-instance sharing creates a real collision risk if A’s outputs are used to steer edits. The lack of locking details pushes this above low.
conditions: IF two B instances operate on the same repo or git branch
IF A-generated instructions are used to trigger overlapping edits
mitigations: Run only one B instance per repository
Use separate branches for parallel work
Pause auto-apply during concurrent edits
Add a manual review step before git writes
Serialize any A→B task handoff

D_cascading_error.rationale: B is a coding agent with review-then-apply and optional auto-apply, so it may treat A’s content as input for code changes or actions. A is a content-writing agent, which makes it plausible that B consumes A’s output without strong verification. This is not high because no downstream external action like email or deployment is documented.
conditions: IF B uses A’s output as the basis for edits or commits
IF auto-apply is enabled in B
mitigations: Require B to cite source lines before editing
Disable auto-apply
Have a human approve each plan step
Ask B to restate A’s output in its own words before acting
Limit B to staging changes only

E_compliance.rationale: No specific regulated data class, residency mismatch, or retention policy is documented for A or B. A is an unverified docs-only content tool, while B handles source code and model-provider API keys; that creates some policy surface, but the rubric’s stronger compliance triggers are not evidenced. I cite both because the pair’s combined handling context matters, though the gap is mostly absence of evidence.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed into B’s project directory
IF organizational policy forbids source-code or API-key processing by external model providers
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of the workspace
Confirm retention settings for any cloud model provider
Document which data classes B may process
Rotate any exposed API keys
Use a local-only environment for sensitive projects
